The Southern bog lemming (Synaptomys cooperi) is a small arvicoline rodent that exhibits a suite of life-history traits typical of subnivean-dwelling species. Females produce litters of three pups [N_R_i = litters of three pups], and under optimal thermal conditions at 37.8 °C [T = 37.8 °C] they can produce approximately 2.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.5 litters per year], representing a relatively high reproductive output for a rodent of its body size. This rapid reproductive rate is likely an adaptation to high juvenile mortality in the ephemeral wet meadows and bogs that constitute its primary habitat. Neonates emerge from the reproductive tract at a wet weight at birth of just 3.46 grams [Wwb = 3.46 grams], a mass consistent with the altricial state of newborn microtine rodents, which are born hairless and with closed eyes. This initial mass is roughly one-seventh of the average weaning weight, indicating substantial maternal investment during the nursing period.

The species' developmental schedule has been documented under controlled laboratory conditions that maintain a stable internal temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. Gestation time spans 23 days [tg = 23 days], a period that is brief relative to many other eutherian mammals of comparable adult size and which facilitates the rapid succession of litters observed during the breeding season at a temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. The postpartum estrus common among arvicolines allows females to become pregnant again almost immediately following parturition, contributing to their high annual fecundity. Field studies have noted that this short gestation is energetically demanding for lactating females, as they must simultaneously support the developing embryos in utero while provisioning the current litter through milk production. The synchrony of these events underscores the physiological intensity of reproduction in this species.

Weaning marks a critical transition in the life cycle of Synaptomys cooperi, and under the same thermal regime of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], the pups achieve nutritional independence at 23 days after birth [tx = 23 days after birth]. At this point, the young have attained a wet weight at weaning of approximately 20 grams [Wwx = approximately 20 grams], a value that represents a nearly sixfold increase over their birth mass. The shift from a milk-based diet to the consumption of grasses, sedges, and other fibrous vegetation coincides with the eruption of molar teeth, a prerequisite for processing tough plant material. This weaning age is relatively short, suggesting that the energetic burden on the mother is alleviated quickly, allowing her to redirect resources toward subsequent litters.

Puberty in female Southern bog lemmings, studied at the species-typical core temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], occurs at 35 days after birth [tp = 35 days after birth], meaning that females are capable of breeding just days after weaning their own cohort. This early reproductive maturity, combined with the short gestation period, allows young-of-the-year born early in the spring to contribute to the late-summer population peak. It is worth noting that this data point for time since birth at puberty is specifically for females, while equivalent values for males remain less certain. The onset of ovarian cyclicity at this age is remarkably rapid, and contrasts with the longer developmental periods observed in larger-bodied arvicolines such as muskrat and beaver. This rapid maturation is a classic correlate of r-selected life-history strategies.

Estimates of maximum longevity for Synaptomys cooperi remain somewhat uncertain, but available data, recorded at a body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 2.5 years [am = approximately 2.5 years]. This relatively short life expectancy is typical for small mammals that experience high predation pressure from raptors, mustelids, and snakes. The ultimate adult wet weight attained by fully grown individuals reaches around 27 grams [Wwi = around 27 grams], a modest size that places the species among the smaller members of the subfamily Arvicolinae. Consistent with its short lifespan and early reproduction, the Southern bog lemming exhibits a high turnover rate in its wild populations. The species' life history stands in instructive contrast to that of larger, longer-lived arvicolids, where delayed reproduction and greater investment per offspring prevail.
